Senses.Explanation: A dry shit-stick is the latrine wiping-tool named by the compound. Linji Yixuan asks what dry shit-stick the person of no rank is; Deshan Xuanjian predicates it of old Shakyamuni; and Yunmen Wenyan asks what dry shit-stick an assembly seeks to chew. In Yunmen’s famous case it answers ‘What is Buddha?’ Wumen Huikai preserves Yunmen as the answerer, Dahui Zonggao repeats the case in verse, and Zhongfeng Mingben places it beside the courtyard cypress and three catties of hemp as sayings with no route for explanatory boring. Wanpu Zhao later asks Miyun Yuanwu what it is and receives only ‘Look on the field ridge.’ The records deploy the named wiping-tool in questions, predicates, answers, case titles, and commentary; they assign it no further stable gloss, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: Compound/object control follows the guide’s calibration: dry + excrement + stick names the latrine wiping-tool, while the corpus does not warrant claims about a particular material construction or a menu of symbolic readings. Seven exact witnesses from seven distinct works.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records make the top of a hundred-foot pole the place where gaining entry is still insufficient and a further step is demanded, questioned, or refused. Changsha Jingcen’s verse says that even one who has gained entry is not yet genuine and must step forward from the pole-top, with the ten directions as the whole body. Wumen transmits Shishuang’s question asking how to advance, and Fojian Huiqin comments on the moment of advancement. An unnamed monastic puts the fixed question to Fadeng, while Yanguan Qi’an counters by asking what use advancement would have. These divergent responses preserve the pole-top as a public challenge rather than a fixed ladder stage.

Senses.Explanation: Zhong Kui is the legendary demon-queller, attested 70 times in 43 allowlisted texts. Chan records do not retell a complete outside biography; they put his name and familiar attributes to work in public answers, festival speech, verse, and appraisal. Asked for “the host within the guest,” Wuzu Fayan answers, “Zhong Kui's little sister” (鍾馗小妹). At the Double-Fifth festival, after a student says that a little ghost might display a trick, Wuzu Fayan replies, “Zhong Kui will frighten you” (鍾馗嚇你), then speaks of a protective talisman. Xiaoyin Xin makes the demon-queller dance eighteen beats (鍾馗解舞十八拍); Panshan Dabo Qian pictures him on a wall beside swords hanging in space (壁上畵鍾馗，空中懸劍戟); and Fushan Fayuan says at New Year that no strange thing is presently before them, so there is no need to paste up Zhong Kui (目前無異怪，不用貼鍾馗). His name can also be an unglossed answer: asked how to discuss words with no trace, Dongshan Shouchu says, “Zhong Kui does not read books” (鍾馗不讀書). The Zen-specific bend is this repeated deployment of the demon-catching figure, his household, dance, painted image, and protective posting as encounter answers and teaching-seat language; no further symbolic meaning is assigned.
